input.question: How was the NASA mission Magellan able to map the Venusian surface so quickly?
input.ground_truth: Venus’ day is 243 earth days long. Magellan orbited Venus every 3 hours or so. That means that during a single Venusian day, the probe circled the planet almost 2000 times. I don’t know what you mean by quickly, but it took almost an entire earth year to get that 96%, for what it’s worth.

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine Venus is like a big, cloudy cake that you can’t see through. The clouds are so thick that you can’t see the cake underneath. But you really want to know what the cake looks like under all those clouds.

Now, NASA sent a spaceship called Magellan to visit Venus. Magellan didn’t have a knife to cut through the clouds, but it had something even better: **radar**. Radar is like a special flashlight that sends out invisible beams and “sees” what bounces back, even through clouds!

So, Magellan flew around Venus and sent out lots of radar beams. These beams bounced off the surface of Venus and came back to Magellan. By looking at how the beams bounced, Magellan could figure out what the surface looked like—mountains, valleys, and all!

Because radar can see through clouds and works day and night, Magellan could map the whole planet very quickly, like taking a picture of the whole cake without even having to see it directly!

So, Magellan used its “special flashlight” (radar) to see through the clouds and take pictures of Venus really fast!
